plan.contextChunk: This figure stacks five drawings of the same fixed string. At the top a horizontal line runs between two black endpoint dots, each labeled "Node", with a double-headed dimension arrow above it labeled L. Beneath come four standing-wave patterns on lines of that same length, labeled at the left n = 1, n = 2, n = 3, and n = 4. Each is a dark blue curve with a pale mirror-image curve, the two outlining the envelope the string sweeps, ends pinned and interior crossing points rising from none to three. Two expressions sit to the right of each: 1/2 lambda_1 = L and lambda_1 = 2/1 L, then lambda_2 = L and lambda_2 = 2/2 L, then 3/2 lambda_3 = L and lambda_3 = 2/3 L, then 4/2 lambda_4 = L and lambda_4 = 2/4 L. A general statement closes the lower right, lambda_n = 2/n L for n = 1, 2, 3, and so on. Holding one length fixed while packing in more half-wavelengths shows how the pinned ends restrict which wavelengths fit. The sequence introduces the normal modes of a string fixed at both ends.

interactionPlan.concept: A string fixed at both ends restricts allowed standing waves to normal modes where an exact integer number of half-wavelengths fits within the string's length.
elements: Top reference line representing the unperturbed string
Black endpoint dots on the reference line labeled 'Node'
Double-headed dimension arrow above the reference line labeled 'L'
Dynamic solid dark blue wave curve representing the current string displacement
Dynamic pale blue mirror-image curve representing the wave's maximum displacement envelope
Interior node dots (black) appearing where the dynamic wave crosses the center line
Dynamic mode label at the left: 'n = 1', 'n = 2', etc.
Dynamic fraction equation at the right: e.g., '1/2 λ_1 = L'
Dynamic wavelength equation at the right: e.g., 'λ_1 = 2/1 L'
General formula label at bottom right: 'λ_n = 2/n L, n = 1, 2, 3, ...'

interactions.label: Mode (n)
interactions.teaches: Stepping through higher mode numbers packs more half-wavelengths into the same fixed length L, introducing interior nodes and reducing the wavelength.

interactions.label: Play oscillation
interactions.teaches: During oscillation, the interior and endpoint nodes remain perfectly stationary while the antinodes sweep between the bounds of the pale blue envelope.

interactions.label: String length (L)
interactions.teaches: Changing the boundary conditions (the distance between fixed endpoints) forces the allowed wavelengths to stretch or compress proportionally, maintaining the λ_n = 2L/n relationship.

demo_steps.title: The Fundamental Mode
demo_steps.narration: The simplest standing wave (n = 1) fits exactly one half-wavelength between the fixed ends. No interior points are stationary.

demo_steps.title: Higher Harmonics
demo_steps.narration: Step to n = 3. Now three half-wavelengths fit in the same space. Notice the appearance of two stationary interior nodes.

demo_steps.title: Stretching the String
demo_steps.narration: Increase the string length L. The mode (n = 3) stays the same, but the wavelength stretches proportionally to accommodate the new physical boundary.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Because the ends of a fixed string cannot move (nodes), only wavelengths that fit a whole number of half-waves exactly into the string length L can form stable standing waves.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Instead of a static stack of four waves, consolidate into a single dynamic wave view. At the top, show the straight reference string and L dimension marker. Below it, draw the selected mode's wave envelope (pale blue) and oscillating solid wave (dark blue). As the 'stringLength' slider moves, scale the horizontal widths of both the L marker and the wave plot. As 'modeNumber' state changes, adjust the sine wave frequency, redraw the interior black node dots, and update the n and λ text equations on the right to match.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Button/state for mode number: the learner steps through n = 1, 2, 3, and 4, the standing-wave shape, interior nodes, and wavelength equation update, making clear that exactly n half-wavelengths must fit inside length L.
- Animation for the selected mode: the learner presses play for any mode, the string oscillates between the two envelope curves while endpoint and interior nodes stay fixed, making clear the difference between nodes and antinodes.
- Slider for string length L: the learner drags the endpoint separation, the displayed wavelength for the selected mode stretches or contracts with the string, making clear the relationship lambda_n = 2L/n.

authoredContext:
The lab setup shows a string attached to a string vibrator, which oscillates the string with an adjustable frequency f. The other end of the string passes over a frictionless pulley and is tied to a hanging mass. The magnitude of the tension in the string is equal to the weight of the hanging mass. The string has a constant linear density (mass per length) μ and the speed at which a wave travels down the string equals v=FTμ=mgμ another section. The symmetrical boundary conditions (a node at each end) dictate the possible frequencies that can excite standing waves. Starting from a frequency of zero and slowly increasing the frequency, the first mode n=1 appears as shown in the figure. The first mode, also called the fundamental mode or the first harmonic, shows half of a wavelength has formed, so the wavelength is equal to twice the length between the nodes λ1=2L. The standing wave patterns that are possible for a string, the first four of which are shown in the figure, are known as the normal modes, with frequencies known as the normal frequencies. In summary, the first frequency to produce a normal mode is called the fundamental frequency (or first harmonic). Any frequencies above the fundamental frequency are overtones. The second frequency of the n=2 normal mode of the string is the first overtone (or second harmonic). The frequency of the n=3 normal mode is the second overtone (or third harmonic) and so on.

Standing waves created on a string of length L. A node occurs at each end of the string. The nodes are boundary conditions that limit the possible frequencies that excite standing waves. (Note that the amplitudes of the oscillations have been kept constant for visualization. The standing wave patterns possible on the string are known as the normal modes. Conducting this experiment in the lab would result in a decrease in amplitude as the frequency increases.)

Four figures of a string of length L are shown. Each has two waves. The first one has 1 node. It is labeled half lambda 1 = L, lambda 1 = 2 by 1 times L. The second figure has 2 nodes. It is labeled lambda 2 = L, lambda 2 = 2 by 2 times L. The third figure has three nodes. It is labeled 3 by 2 times lambda 3 = L, lambda 3 = 2 by 3 times L. The fourth figure has 4 nodes. It is labeled 4 by 2 times lambda 4 = L, lambda 4 = 2 by 4 times L. There is a derived formula at the bottom, lambda n equal to 2 by n times L for n = 1, 2, 3 and so on.

discrepancies: The generated figure displays only one mode at a time with a large empty vertical gap between the reference string and the wave, rather than stacking all modes compactly as in the source.
The equations are placed at fixed horizontal coordinates far to the right, leaving a large horizontal gap between the wave and the text when the wave is short.
The wave's amplitude is much larger relative to its length compared to the long, slender proportions of the waves in the source.
Dashed vertical alignment lines were added between the reference string and the wave endpoints, which do not appear in the source.
evaluation.notes: The figure successfully converts a static multipanel diagram into a highly interactive, animated simulation, but the layout suffers from excessive whitespace and stubby wave proportions due to hardcoded layout coordinates.
action_items: Dynamically position the equation groups (currently fixed at x1=640 and x2=740) relative to the right edge of the wave (`X0 + L_px + offset`) to eliminate the large horizontal gap.
Reduce the vertical space between the reference string (y=120) and the wave by moving the wave center (`Y_center`) up to around 180.
Decrease the wave amplitude `A` (from 65 to ~35) and increase the base length multiplier (from 300 to ~450) to match the elongated, slender wave proportions of the source.

feedback.rationale: Scores are very high (4s and 5s), there are no failure modes, and the discrepancies are purely minor layout adjustments, indicating the figure is good enough to stop iterating.
